content_voiceover: Cold AIHA works completely differently — it's IgM and complement mediated. IgM antibodies have increased activity around zero degrees Celsius and decreased activity near thirty seven, so they bind C1q and red cells in the cooler peripheral circulation, like the fingertips, nose, and ears. As blood returns to the warmer central circulation, IgM dissociates, but it has already activated the classical complement pathway through C4, C2, and C3, depositing C3b on the red cell surface. C3b-opsonized cells are cleared extravascularly by Kupffer cells in the liver. If complement activation proceeds all the way to C5 through C9, forming the membrane attack complex, that causes direct intravascular hemolysis. Clinically, IgM-mediated agglutination in the cold peripheral vessels produces acrocyanosis or Raynaud's phenomenon. One clinical pearl worth remembering: even a low titer of IgM can trigger significant hemolysis because IgM is such an efficient complement activator — one IgM molecule can fix complement, unlike IgG which usually needs two molecules in proximity.
keypoints: Cold AIHA: IgM binds RBCs + C1q in cold peripheral circulation
IgM dissociates centrally; complement cascade continues (C3b, C5b-9)
C3b → extravascular hemolysis (liver); C5b-9/MAC → intravascular hemolysis
Clinical: acrocyanosis/Raynaud's; low IgM titer still hemolyzes
keypoint_voiceover: Cold AIHA is IgM and complement mediated. IgM binds red cells and fixes C1q in cold peripheral vessels, then dissociates as blood warms, but complement keeps working — C3b drives extravascular hemolysis in the liver, while C5b-9, the membrane attack complex, causes direct intravascular hemolysis. Clinically this produces acrocyanosis or Raynaud's phenomenon, and remember, even a low IgM titer can cause significant hemolysis because one IgM molecule efficiently fixes complement.
